questions.question: A wilderness weather station system emphasizes which constraint most?
options: Streaming high-definition video continuously
Training users with long classroom sessions
Delivering new features daily without testing
Supporting millions of concurrent transactions
Operating reliably with limited remote power
questions.explanation: Remote data collection systems must manage power and withstand harsh conditions.

questions.question: What is a software process in software engineering terms?
options: A structured set of activities to build software
A final executable produced after compilation
A legal contract used to purchase software
A hardware workflow for manufacturing devices
A random set of tasks chosen during coding
questions.explanation: A software process is a structured set of activities used to develop a system.

questions.question: Which item is typically included in a process description?
options: Roles and responsibilities for process participants
Marketing slogans for the product launch
User interface color palette for each screen
CPU instruction timings for each source file
Office seating plan for the development team
questions.explanation: Process descriptions often define activities, outcomes, roles, and entry/exit conditions.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a plan-driven process?
options: Progress is measured by number of meetings held
Progress is measured by lines of code written
Progress is measured by tool popularity online
Progress is measured only by customer mood
Progress is measured against an upfront plan
questions.explanation: Plan-driven processes plan activities in advance and track progress against the plan.

questions.question: In agile development, requirements are typically handled how?
options: Frozen completely before any coding starts
Copied unchanged from earlier unrelated projects
Negotiated continuously as the product evolves
Defined only after final system deployment
Derived solely from regulatory checklists
questions.explanation: Agile expects change and continuously refines requirements during development.

questions.question: Which phase order best matches the waterfall model?
options: Requirements, implementation, maintenance, design, testing
Design, requirements, testing, implementation, maintenance
Requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance
Implementation, testing, requirements, design, maintenance
Testing, requirements, design, maintenance, implementation
questions.explanation: The waterfall model proceeds sequentially from requirements through maintenance.

questions.question: Which issue is a common risk in incremental development without discipline?
options: Early delivery becomes impossible by definition
Requirements become impossible to change later
Architecture degrades without refactoring over time
Testing must be postponed until maintenance phase
Customer feedback cannot occur until the end
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery can lead to erosion of structure unless refactoring is done.

questions.question: What is a typical trade-off when using reuse/configuration with COTS?
options: Some requirements are compromised to fit components
Integration becomes unnecessary by using COTS
System evolution becomes fully under customer control
Testing becomes optional because components exist
All requirements are satisfied without negotiation
questions.explanation: Using existing components speeds delivery but can force requirement compromises and reduce control.

questions.question: Which order best matches typical testing stages?
options: Component testing, system testing, customer testing
System testing, component testing, customer testing
Customer testing, system testing, component testing
Component testing, customer testing, system testing
Customer testing, component testing, system testing
questions.explanation: Testing usually moves from components to the integrated system, then to customer acceptance.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches two change strategies?
options: Anticipation uses marketing; tolerance uses new slogans
Anticipation uses outsourcing; tolerance uses no testing
Anticipation uses prototyping; tolerance uses incremental delivery
Anticipation uses refactoring; tolerance uses freeze-all planning
Anticipation uses contracts; tolerance uses zero documentation
questions.explanation: Prototyping helps anticipate change; incremental delivery helps tolerate ongoing change.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a throw-away prototype?
options: A first release intended to be maintained forever
A final product certified for safety deployment
A complete system built only after full testing
A reused component integrated without any change
A quick model built to learn, then discarded
questions.explanation: Throw-away prototypes are built to clarify requirements and are not intended for production.

questions.question: Which is a common difficulty of incremental delivery?
options: Accommodating requirement changes between increments
Identifying shared services needed across increments
Delivering useful functionality early in the schedule
Reducing risk by prioritizing key requirements first
Obtaining early user feedback on partial releases
questions.explanation: Incremental development can make it harder to plan shared facilities and system-wide infrastructure.

questions.question: Which sequence best matches a basic process improvement cycle?
options: Measure, analyze, change, repeat
Design, deploy, market, repeat
Code, compile, compress, repeat
Purchase, install, license, repeat
Plan, ignore, blame, repeat
questions.explanation: Process improvement typically measures performance, analyzes causes, makes changes, and iterates.

questions.question: Which item is an example of a process metric?
options: Brand popularity of the programming language
Number of defects found per release
Number of fonts used in documentation
Color scheme used in the user interface
Amount of coffee consumed by the team
questions.explanation: Defect counts, effort, time, and resource use are typical process metrics.

questions.question: In the CMMI maturity model, which level is the highest?
options: Managed measured process level
Initial ad-hoc process level
Defined standard process level
Repeatable managed process level
Optimising process improvement level
questions.explanation: The highest CMMI maturity level is Optimising, focused on continuous improvement.

questions.question: Which agile value pairing is stated in the Agile Manifesto?
options: Following a plan over responding to change
Strict phases over continuous integration
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
questions.explanation: The manifesto values people and collaboration, and prioritizes working software and adaptability.

questions.question: Which practice is characteristic of agile development?
options: Maximizing documentation before writing code
Freezing requirements before any design starts
Postponing testing until after deployment
Delivering working increments frequently
Rejecting stakeholder involvement during sprints
questions.explanation: Agile emphasizes frequent delivery of working software with ongoing stakeholder involvement.

questions.question: Which XP practice requires writing tests before code?
options: Document-first delivery practice
Test-driven development practice
Change freeze control practice
Big design upfront practice
Single-integration release practice
questions.explanation: Test-driven development creates tests first, then implements code to make tests pass.

questions.question: Which statement best describes pair programming?
options: Two customers write the entire implementation
Two managers approve each line of code
Two developers work together at one workstation
Two teams work separately without communication
Two releases are merged only at project end
questions.explanation: Pair programming puts two developers together to improve quality and shared understanding.

questions.question: In Scrum, who is responsible for prioritizing the product backlog?
options: The quality assurance role
The operations support role
The development team role
The product owner role
The scrum master role
questions.explanation: The Product Owner manages and prioritizes the Product Backlog.

questions.question: In Scrum, what is a primary responsibility of the Scrum Master?
options: Writing all code for each sprint deliverable
Setting final product requirements unilaterally
Creating hardware deployment diagrams for servers
Removing impediments and supporting Scrum practice
Approving budgets and negotiating legal contracts
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master facilitates Scrum, helps remove blockers, and supports the team’s process.

questions.question: A Scrum sprint is typically which duration range?
options: Twenty to forty weeks long
Two to four years long
Two to four weeks long
Two to four months long
Two to four days long
questions.explanation: Scrum sprints commonly run for about 2–4 weeks.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a Scrum of Scrums?
options: Eliminating integration by separating codebases
Replacing product backlog with fixed contracts
Moving all decisions to a single manager
Coordinating work across multiple Scrum teams
Preventing requirements changes during delivery
questions.explanation: Scrum of Scrums synchronizes and resolves dependencies across teams.

questions.question: When is a plan-driven approach usually more suitable?
options: For innovative products with unclear requirements
For prototypes exploring new user experiences
For startups prioritizing speed over documentation
For small co-located teams with rapid feedback
For safety-critical systems with heavy regulation
questions.explanation: Large, safety-critical, regulated, or long-lived systems often require plan-driven or hybrid approaches.

questions.question: What is requirements engineering primarily concerned with?
options: Establishing required services and constraints
Implementing algorithms and data structures
Training users after the system is deployed
Choosing the best compiler and IDE settings
Selecting hardware parts for device assembly
questions.explanation: It establishes what the system should do and the constraints on operation and development.

questions.question: Which description best matches user requirements?
options: High-level services stated for customer readers
Database schemas stated for administrator readers
Mathematical proofs stated for verifier readers
Source code interfaces stated for programmer readers
Detailed functions stated for developer readers
questions.explanation: User requirements are higher-level, often natural language plus diagrams, written for customers.

questions.question: Which description best matches system requirements?
options: Detailed functions and constraints in a structured form
GUI mockups showing only visual layout decisions
Marketing vision statements with broad aspirations
Informal notes from ad-hoc brainstorming sessions
Unit test suites defining internal code behavior
questions.explanation: System requirements describe detailed functions, services, and constraints and may form part of a contract.

questions.question: Which item is a functional requirement example?
options: The system is developed using a mandated standard
The system complies with applicable privacy laws
The system uses less than 200 MB of memory
The system maintains 99.99% availability weekly
The system can search and list appointments
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe services the system provides and how it reacts to inputs.

questions.question: Which item is a non-functional requirement example?
options: The system stores each patient record as JSON
The system assigns a unique staff identifier
The system schedules an appointment for a patient
The system responds within two seconds per query
The system prints a daily appointment list
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements constrain qualities like performance, reliability, security, and process.

questions.question: Which item is best described as a domain requirement?
options: Database must be PostgreSQL version fifteen
Code must be written in a specific IDE
Insulin dose must not exceed safe limits
User interface must use a dark theme
Sprints must be exactly three weeks long
questions.explanation: Domain requirements come from the application domain and constrain the system’s behavior.

questions.question: Which classification of non-functional requirements is correct?
options: User, manager, and investor categories
Compile-time, runtime, and link-time categories
Static, dynamic, and polymorphic categories
Functional, transactional, and graphical categories
Product, organizational, and external categories
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements can be classified as product, organizational, or external constraints.

questions.question: Which requirement is most verifiable for usability?
options: Interface is easy to use for everyone
System is intuitive without any instruction
Usability is perfect across all situations
Training time under four hours for new users
Users will love the interface immediately
questions.explanation: Replacing vague goals with measurable criteria makes requirements verifiable.

questions.question: Which elicitation technique involves observing real work practices?
options: Closed questionnaire technique
Version control technique
Ethnography observation technique
Code inspection technique
Formal proof technique
questions.explanation: Ethnography studies how people actually work to uncover tacit requirements.

questions.question: Which interview style tends to elicit richer qualitative detail?
options: Binary choice-only interview style
Closed yes-no question interview style
Open-ended question interview style
Scripted monologue-only interview style
Silent observation-only interview style
questions.explanation: Open-ended questions encourage stakeholders to explain context, goals, and exceptions.

questions.question: Which set lists common requirements validation checks?
options: Secrecy, obscurity, complexity, opacity, ambiguity
Throughput, latency, jitter, bandwidth, routing
Validity, consistency, realism, verifiability, completeness
Profitability, popularity, novelty, branding, aesthetics
Syntax, parsing, linking, compiling, packaging
questions.explanation: Validation checks that requirements reflect real needs, are consistent, feasible, complete enough, and testable.

questions.question: Fixing requirements errors after delivery is often how much more expensive?
options: Roughly one hundred times more expensive
Roughly one tenth the earlier cost
Roughly ten times more expensive
Roughly two times more expensive
Roughly the same cost as before
questions.explanation: Late discovery multiplies costs because it requires rework, retesting, redeployment, and user disruption.

questions.question: What is a primary purpose of requirements traceability?
options: Replacing validation with informal stakeholder trust
Removing the need for version management tools
Preventing any future requirements changes entirely
Linking requirements to design, code, and tests
Ensuring every requirement is implemented twice
questions.explanation: Traceability supports impact analysis and controlled change by tracking where requirements are realized.

questions.question: Which section is commonly part of a requirements document?
options: A server rack diagram showing cable routes
A build log listing compiler warnings
A marketing plan for feature promotion
A payroll sheet listing employee salaries
A glossary defining key domain terms
questions.explanation: Requirements documents often include introductions, glossaries, user/system requirements, and supporting material.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of system modeling?
options: Creating documents to replace stakeholder discussion
Creating implementation details instead of requirements
Creating diagrams to guarantee zero defects
Creating final code without any intermediate models
Creating abstract views for stakeholder understanding
questions.explanation: Models provide simplified perspectives to analyze, communicate, and reason about a system.

questions.question: Which set lists the four key modeling perspectives?
options: Budget, staffing, marketing, sales
Compile, link, load, execute
Context, interaction, structure, behavior
CPU, memory, disk, network
Syntax, semantics, pragmatics, phonetics
questions.explanation: Modeling commonly considers external context, interactions, structural organization, and behavior over time.

questions.question: Which UML diagram is best for showing actors and system goals?
options: Deployment diagram representation
Use case diagram representation
Package diagram representation
State diagram representation
Class diagram representation
questions.explanation: Use case diagrams show interactions between external actors and the system’s use cases.

questions.question: In a sequence diagram, how is time typically represented?
options: Time progresses horizontally from left to right
Time is shown through hardware deployment nodes
Time is omitted to reduce diagram complexity
Time is encoded only through color selection
Time progresses vertically from top to bottom
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams place objects across the top and show time flowing downward.

questions.question: In a class diagram, what does generalization represent?
options: It represents communication through database queries
It represents transitions between states on events
It represents links between actors and use cases
It represents forks and joins in workflows
It represents inheritance from superclass to subclass
questions.explanation: Generalization models inheritance relationships between classes.

questions.question: In a class diagram, what does aggregation represent?
options: A part-of relationship between whole and part
A mandatory dependency on a specific platform
A requirement that every object has one state
A complete replacement of one class by another
A sequence of messages exchanged over time
questions.explanation: Aggregation models a whole–part relationship, typically a weaker form of composition.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches diagram to behavior type?
options: Sequence diagram for data-driven flow; context diagram for event-driven change
Class diagram for data-driven flow; use case diagram for event-driven change
Activity diagram for data-driven flow; state diagram for event-driven change
Use case diagram for data-driven flow; class diagram for event-driven change
State diagram for data-driven flow; activity diagram for event-driven change
questions.explanation: Activity diagrams model workflows; state diagrams model event-triggered state transitions.

questions.question: What does a context model primarily show?
options: Source code style rules for each module
Runtime state transitions for a single object
Internal class attributes and method signatures
System boundary and external interacting systems
Detailed message order for one scenario
questions.explanation: Context models define what is outside the system and the external systems it interacts with.

questions.question: Which limitation is commonly associated with model-driven engineering?
options: Strong dependency on specialized tooling
Removal of need for requirements engineering
Complete inability to represent interactions
Automatic elimination of all platform concerns
Guaranteed perfect alignment with agile values
questions.explanation: MDE can raise abstraction but often relies heavily on tools and can be hard to adopt.

questions.question: Which transformation order is typical in model-driven architecture?
options: PSM to PIM to CIM to code
CIM to PIM to PSM to code
CIM to PSM to PIM to code
Code to PSM to PIM to CIM
PIM to CIM to PSM to code
questions.explanation: MDA typically refines from a computation-independent model to platform-independent, then platform-specific, then code.

questions.question: Why might an incomplete model still be acceptable early on?
options: It guarantees full requirement consistency
It enables direct code generation immediately
It eliminates later validation activities
It prevents any future design change
It supports discussion despite missing details
questions.explanation: Early models can be partial if their purpose is communication and exploration.

questions.question: What does software architecture primarily define?
options: Defining marketing plans for distribution
Defining exact code for every function
Defining training material for end users
Defining laptop operating systems for developers
Defining major components and their interactions
questions.explanation: Architecture captures the high-level system structure, components, and interactions.

questions.question: Why are architectural decisions expensive to change later?
options: They affect only one module in isolation
They only affect unit tests and test data files
They affect many components and cross-cutting concerns
They only affect color choices and screen layout
They affect only compiler flags and build scripts
questions.explanation: Core architectural changes ripple across components, interfaces, deployment, and quality properties.

questions.question: In the 4+1 architectural view model, which view focuses on runtime processes?
options: Scenario view of validating use cases
Physical view of deployment hardware
Development view of code organization
Process view of runtime concurrency
Logical view of key abstractions
questions.explanation: The process view describes how the system is composed of interacting processes at run time.

questions.question: Why can adopting MDA/MDE be difficult in practice?
options: It guarantees perfect alignment with agile values
It removes the need for requirements engineering
It needs specialized tools and heavy upfront models
It prevents any change once modeling begins
It cannot represent system context in any form
questions.explanation: Tooling needs and extensive upfront modeling can make adoption difficult and conflict with agile practices.

questions.question: Which architectural choice most directly supports security layering?
options: Pipe-and-filter structure for interactive tasks
Single component structure for all functions
Flat structure with unrestricted global access
Layered structure with protected inner layers
Random structure changed each iteration
questions.explanation: Layering can protect critical assets by placing them in inner layers with controlled access.

questions.question: Which statement best matches the fault–error–failure relationship?
options: Error and failure are identical by definition
Fault can cause error; error can cause failure
Failure can cause error; error can cause fault
Error can cause fault; fault can cause failure
Fault and failure always occur together
questions.explanation: A fault may lead to an error state, and an error may lead to an externally visible failure.

questions.question: Which UML model best shows event-driven state transitions of an object?
options: State diagram showing states and transitions
Context model showing system boundary
Use case diagram showing actor goals
Activity diagram showing workflow steps
Class diagram showing static relationships
questions.explanation: State diagrams model how an object changes state in response to events.

questions.question: In socio-technical systems, what is a major single cause of failures?
options: Human operational mistakes during system use
Formal methods applied too early
Redundancy used in every subsystem
Hardware that never ages or degrades
Perfectly correct software specifications
questions.explanation: Operational failures caused by human mistakes are a major contributor in socio-technical systems.

questions.question: Using COTS most directly shifts design focus toward what activity?
options: Eliminating all stakeholder communication
Avoiding any modeling before implementation
Proving correctness through formal methods
Replacing testing with vendor reputation
Configuring features to meet requirements
questions.explanation: With COTS, design often becomes selecting and configuring existing capabilities rather than coding everything.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches model type to perspective?
options: Context model for tests; interaction model for budgets
Context model for code; interaction model for licensing
Context model for workflow; interaction model for deployment
Context model for states; interaction model for classes
Context model for environment; interaction model for exchanges
questions.explanation: Context models show boundaries and external systems, while interaction models show exchanges with users or systems.

questions.question: Why is defect-testing data often unsuitable for reliability testing?
options: It ignores specifications during test design
It replaces test cases with formal proofs
It mismatches the real operational input distribution
It ignores time between failures as a measure
It forbids failures during any test execution
questions.explanation: Reliability testing needs an operational profile that reflects real usage patterns, unlike many defect tests.

questions.question: Which definition best matches availability?
options: Probability code compiles without warnings today
Probability system runs failure-free over an interval
Probability system is operational at a time point
Probability users approve the interface immediately
Probability requirements are complete at delivery
questions.explanation: Availability is the likelihood the system is up and able to deliver useful service at a given time.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes reliability and availability?
options: Reliability is up now; availability is failure-free over time
Reliability is failure-free over time; availability is up now
Reliability and availability are identical in every system
Reliability equals security only; availability equals safety only
Reliability is subjective always; availability is subjective always
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free operation over a period, while availability concerns being operational at a point in time.

questions.question: Which statement about reuse levels is correct?
options: Object reuse reuses only entire application systems
Abstraction reuse reuses successful design ideas
System reuse reuses only single library objects
Component reuse reuses only database schemas
Reuse always eliminates integration and adaptation
questions.explanation: Abstraction-level reuse means reusing design knowledge and patterns that worked well before.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes redundancy and diversity?
options: Redundancy and diversity mean the same thing
Redundancy only hardware; diversity only software
Redundancy adds backups; diversity varies implementations
Redundancy adds testing; diversity reduces testing
Redundancy varies implementations; diversity adds backups
questions.explanation: Redundancy provides backup components, while diversity reduces common-mode failures by varying implementations.

questions.question: Which pattern matches a shared central data store used by subsystems?
options: Repository pattern with a central store
Client–server pattern with remote requests
Pipe-and-filter pattern with streaming transforms
Layered pattern with strict service levels
MVC pattern with separated presentation
questions.explanation: The repository pattern centralizes shared data accessed by multiple components.

questions.question: Which reliability metric best fits infrequent demand services?
options: POFOD probability of failure on demand
AVAIL fraction of time operational
MTTF mean time to failure
ROCOF rate of occurrence of failures
LOC lines of code total
questions.explanation: POFOD measures the chance of failure when a demand occurs, useful for intermittent critical functions.

questions.question: Compared with a use case overview, what does a sequence diagram add?
options: Ordering of object interactions over time
Regulatory approvals and certification plan
Static class attributes and inheritance trees
Hardware nodes and network topology layout
List of stakeholders and organizational politics
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams show the detailed message ordering between objects for a scenario instance.

questions.question: Which characteristic is typical of dependable development processes?
options: Unstandardized and untracked change activities
Ad-hoc and undocumented development activities
Unmeasured and unreviewed development activities
Repeatable and auditable development activities
Single-person skill dependent development activities
questions.explanation: Dependable processes are defined, repeatable, auditable, and supported by systematic verification and documentation.

questions.question: Which statement best captures what safety means?
options: Avoiding reuse to prevent dependencies
Avoiding failures under normal conditions
Avoiding documentation during development
Avoiding harm even under abnormal conditions
Avoiding change during system evolution
questions.explanation: Safety is about preventing injury or damage, which is not the same as simply meeting the specification.

questions.question: How can a system be reliable yet unsafe?
options: It has perfect availability and perfect security
It has no users and no environment
It follows an incorrect specification consistently
It has no specification and no implementation
It follows a correct specification inconsistently
questions.explanation: A system can behave exactly as specified, but still be unsafe if the specification omits safety constraints.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches safety-critical system type to example?
options: Primary: web store; secondary: video game system
Primary: insulin pump; secondary: medical records system
Primary: batch payroll; secondary: compiler system
Primary: CAD tool; secondary: email client system
Primary: spreadsheet; secondary: photo editor system
questions.explanation: Primary safety-critical systems directly threaten life on failure; secondary can trigger harmful failures elsewhere.

questions.question: What is a hazard in safety engineering terms?
options: A bug that always causes immediate failure
A requirement that guarantees full availability
A test case that proves a program correct
A security patch applied after deployment
A condition that could lead to an accident
questions.explanation: A hazard is a system condition with the potential to cause an accident.

questions.question: Risk is best described as which combination?
options: Combination of schedule and budget constraints
Combination of encryption and authentication methods
Combination of usability and performance metrics
Combination of hazard probability and severity
Combination of code style and documentation detail
questions.explanation: Risk combines how likely a hazard is and how severe the consequences could be.

questions.question: In hazard assessment, what does ALARP represent?
options: Risk eliminated by definition through compliance
Risk increased to maximize test coverage
Risk reduced as low as reasonably practicable
Risk accepted as large and unavoidable permanently
Risk ignored until after system deployment
questions.explanation: ALARP is a middle category where risk must be reduced as far as reasonably practicable.

questions.question: Which set lists core strategies for achieving safety?
options: Recruitment, promotion, compensation, retention
Refactoring, optimization, parallelization, caching
Feature growth, market fit, brand expansion
Hazard avoidance, hazard removal, damage limitation
Compilation, linking, loading, execution
